questions.knowledge_point: Finding the First Term Exceeding a Given Value
questions.problem:
What is the first term that exceeds  $2\,000$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
\,\,\,\,10,\,15,\,\frac{45}{2},\,\frac{135}{4},\,…
$$

The first term that exceeds $2\,000$ is the
{{field-1}}th term.
questions.worked_solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=10$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{15}{10}=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =10\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $2000.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & >2000 \\ 10\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1} & >2000 \\ {(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1} & >200 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(200) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(200) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(200)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(200)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(200)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})}+1≈14.067.
$$

Therefore, the $15$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $2000.$

questions.problem:
What is the first term that is less than $0.004$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
20,\,4,\,\frac{4}{5},\,\frac{4}{25},\,…
$$

The first term that is less than $0.004$ is the
{{field-1}}th term.
questions.worked_solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=20$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{4}{20}=\frac{1}{5}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =20{(\frac{1}{5})}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be less than $0.004.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & <0.004 \\ 20{(\frac{1}{5})}^{n-1} & <0.004 \\ {(\frac{1}{5})}^{n-1} & <\frac{0.004}{20} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(\frac{1}{5})}^{n-1} & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,2) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{1}{5}) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,2) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,2)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{1}{5})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,2)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{1}{5})}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we reversed the inequality sign when divided by $\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{1}{5})$ because $\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{1}{5})$ is a negative number. 

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,2)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{1}{5})}+1≈6.292.
$$

Therefore, the $7$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0.004.$

questions.problem:
What is the first term that is less than $0.000\,6$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
64,\,32,\,16,\,8,\,…
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=64$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{32}{64}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =64\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{n-1} \\  & ={2}^{6}\cdot {2}^{1-n} \\  & ={2}^{7-n}\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be less than $0.000\,6.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & <0.000\,6 \\ {2}^{7-n} & <0.000\,6 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(2)}^{7-n} & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,6) \\ (7-n)\operatorname{log}⁡(2) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,6) \\ 7-n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,6)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)} \\ -n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,6)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}-7 \\ n & >7-\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,6)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
7-\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,6)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}≈17.703
$$

Therefore, the $18$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0.000\,6.$

questions.problem:
The $2$nd term of a geometric sequence with a positive common ratio is $\frac{3}{2}$, and the $4$th term is $\frac{2}{3}.$ Given that all terms of the sequence are positive, what is the first term of this sequence to be less than
$0.000\,11?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that ${a}_{2}=\frac{3}{2}$ and ${a}_{4}=\frac{2}{3}$, we can find the common ratio $r$ of the sequence, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{n-m} & =\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}} \\ {r}^{4-2} & =\frac{{a}_{4}}{{a}_{2}} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{\frac{2}{3}}{\frac{3}{2}} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{4}{9} \\ r & =\pm \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the common ratio is positive, we take the positive value. Now, since ${a}_{4}=\frac{2}{3}$ and  $r=\frac{2}{3}$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for ${a}_{1}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{4} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{2}{3})}^{4-1} \\ \frac{2}{3} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{2}{3})}^{3} \\ {(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & ={a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\cdot {(\frac{2}{3})}^{n-1} \\  & ={(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{1-n} \\  & ={(\frac{3}{2})}^{3-n}\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be less than $0.000\,11.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{3}{2})}^{3-n} & <0.000\,11 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(\frac{3}{2})}^{3-n} & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,11) \\ (3-n)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2}) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,11) \\ 3-n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,11)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})} \\ -n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,11)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})}-3 \\ n & >3-\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,11)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
3-\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,11)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})}≈25.480
$$

Therefore, the $26$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0.000\,11.$

questions.problem:

$907?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that ${a}_{6}=3$ and  $r=3$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for ${a}_{1}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{6} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {3}^{6-1} \\ 3 & ={a}_{1}\cdot {3}^{5} \\ \frac{1}{{3}^{4}} & ={a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =\frac{1}{81}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{81}\cdot {3}^{n-1} \\  & ={3}^{-4}\cdot {3}^{n-1} \\  & ={3}^{n-5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want $n$th term to be greater than $907.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{n-5} & >907 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(3)}^{n-5} & >\operatorname{log}⁡(907) \\ (n-5)\operatorname{log}⁡(3) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(907) \\ n-5 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(907)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(907)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}+5\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(907)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}+5≈11.199
$$

Therefore, the $12$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $907.$

questions.problem:
The $3$rd term of a geometric sequence is $5$, and the $6$th term is $40.$ What is the first term of this sequence to exceed
$2\,020?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that ${a}_{3}=5$ and ${a}_{6}=40$, we can find the common ratio $r$ of the sequence, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{n-m} & =\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}} \\ {r}^{6-3} & =\frac{{a}_{6}}{{a}_{3}} \\ {r}^{3} & =\frac{40}{5} \\ {r}^{3} & =8 \\ r & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since ${a}_{3}=5$ and  $r=2$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for ${a}_{1}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{3} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {2}^{3-1} \\ 5 & ={a}_{1}\cdot {2}^{2} \\ 5 & =4{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\cdot {2}^{n-1} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{{2}^{2}}\cdot {2}^{n-1} \\  & =5\cdot {2}^{n-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want $n$th term to be greater than $2\,020.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}5\cdot {2}^{n-3} & >2\,020 \\ {2}^{n-3} & >404 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{2}^{n-3} & >\operatorname{log}⁡(404) \\ (n-3)\operatorname{log}⁡(2) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(404) \\ n-3 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(404)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(404)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}+3\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(404)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}+3≈11.658
$$

Therefore, the $12$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $2\,020.$

questions.problem:
The $4$th term of a geometric sequence is $108$, and the common ratio is $\frac{3}{2}.$ What is the first term of this sequence to exceed
$1\,984?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that ${a}_{4}=108$ and  $r=\frac{3}{2}$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for ${a}_{1}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{4} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{4-1} \\ 108 & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{3} \\ 108 & =\frac{27}{8}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =32\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =32\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want $n$th term to be greater than $1\,984.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}32\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1} & >1\,984 \\ {(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1} & >62 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1} & >\operatorname{log}⁡(62) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(62) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(62)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(62)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(62)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})}+1≈11.179
$$

Therefore, the $12$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $1\,984.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the First Term Exceeding a Given Value
canonical_examples.problem:
What is the first term that exceeds $2\,000\,000$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
\dfrac 1 {32},\: \dfrac 1 4,\: 2,\: 16,\: \ldots
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The first term of the sequence is $a_1=\dfrac{1}{32}$ and the common ratio is

$$
r = \dfrac {\left(\dfrac 1 {4}\right)} {\left(\dfrac 1 {32} \right)} = 8.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{32}\cdot {8}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{2}{64}\cdot {8}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{2}{{8}^{2}}\cdot {8}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {8}^{-2}\cdot {8}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {8}^{n-3}\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $2\,000\,000.$ So, we set up and solve the corresponding inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot {8}^{n-3} & >2\,000\,000 \\ {8}^{n-3} & >1\,000\,000 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({8}^{n-3}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000) \\ (n-3)\operatorname{log}⁡(8) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000) \\ n-3 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(8)} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(8)}+3\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\dfrac {\log (1\,000\, 000)} {\log (8)} + 3 \approx 9.643.
$$

Therefore, the $10$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $2\,000\,000.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the First Term Smaller Than a Given Value
canonical_examples.problem:
What is the first term that is less than $0. 000\,000\,1$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
16,\: 8,\: 4,\: 2,\: \ldots
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The first term of the sequence is $a_1=16,$ and the common ratio is

$$
r = \dfrac 8 {16}  = \dfrac 1 2.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =16\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{n-1} \\  & ={2}^{4}\cdot {2}^{1-n} \\  & ={2}^{5-n}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be less than $0.000\,000\,1.$ So, we set up and solve the corresponding inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{5-n} & <0.000\,000\,1 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({2}^{5-n}) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,000\,1) \\ (5-n)\operatorname{log}⁡(2) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,000\,1) \\ 5-n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,000\,1)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)} \\ -n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,000\,1)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}-5 \\ n & >5-\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,000\,1)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
5 - \dfrac { \log (0.000\, 000\, 1)} {\log (2)} \approx 28.253.
$$

Therefore, the $29$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0. 000\,000\,1.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Cases Where the First Term Is Unknown
canonical_examples.problem:
The $4$th term of a geometric sequence is $54,$ and the common ratio is $3.$ What is the first term of this sequence to exceed
$1\,000?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since we are given that $a_{4}= 54$ and  $r= 3,$ we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for $a_1,$ as follows:

$$
\eqalign{a_n&=a_1\cdot r^{n-1}\[3pt]
		a_4&=a_1\cdot 3^{4-1}\[3pt]
	54&=a_1\cdot 3^3\[3pt]
	54&=27a_1\[3pt]
	a_1&=2
	}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {3}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $1\,000.$ So, we set up and solve the corresponding inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot {3}^{n-1} & >1\,000 \\ {3}^{n-1} & >500 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡(3)^{n-1} & >\operatorname{log}⁡(500) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(3) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(500) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(500)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(500)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\dfrac {\log (500)} {\log (3)} + 1 \approx 6.657.
$$

Therefore, the $7$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $1\,000.$
